                                             PROJECT NO. 58482

    LARGE LOAD DEMAND                                        §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    MANAGEMENT SERVICE                                       §
                                                             §                         OF TEXAS

                                        COMMENTS OF
                              TEXAS ELECTRIC COOPERATIVES, INC.

           Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. (TEC) respectfully submits these comments in response

to the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUC or Commission) proposal for publication (PFP)

regarding the Large Load Demand Management Service (LLDMS).1 TEC is the statewide

association of electric cooperatives operating in Texas, representing its members except as their

interests may be separately represented.2 The PFP directed comments to be filed by September 4.

These comments are timely filed.

                                             I.        Staff Questions

1.         Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling entity
           representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is
           subject to availability verification during the Large Load Demand Management
           Service (LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large load customer that is available
           but not ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be
           compensated some percentage of the market clearing price for the large load
           customer' s availability to reduce demand during the LLDMS obligation period? If
           so, what is an appropriate payment to the large load customer for their availability
           during the LLDMS obligation period?

           TEC believes it may be appropriate to allocate a portion of the LLDMS budget for

readiness payments that ensure a large load is ready to be turned off when needed. A readiness

payment should be a small percentage of the clearing price, with most of the LLDMS budget




1
    Proposal for Publication New §25.521 (Jul. 30, 2026) (PFP).
2
  TEC’s 78 members include distribution cooperatives that provide retail electric utility service to approximately
5,000,000 consumers in statutorily authorized service areas that encompass more than half of the total area of the state.
TEC’s G&T members generally acquire generation resources and power supply for their member distribution
cooperatives and deliver electricity to them at wholesale.



                                                                                                                       1
 allocated for actual performance payments. Both payment types will be necessary, because a

readiness payment and a performance payment incentivize different activities.

        A readiness payment induces a resource to be ready to respond when directed. A high

readiness payment may incentivize more large loads to sign up for or indicate their willingness to

be in the LLDMS, but without a corresponding inducement for actual performance, the service

will likely result in expensive non-performance unless claw backs are utilized as well.

        A performance payment incentivizes the actual performance when needed during an

emergency condition. Large computational loads are typically constant users of power, meaning

they will need to plan ahead and have a performance plan in place if they are to effectively

participate in LLDMS. This need to plan ahead in order to participate lends itself to a readiness

payment. Performance payments without readiness may still garner some sporadic participation,

but program success will be limited by those large loads that are not ready or prepared to respond

when called upon. Both performance and readiness payments will be needed to incentivize proper

preparation before and adequate performance during an event.

2.      Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a calendar
        year. What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

        No response at this time.

3.      What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how
        far in advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?

        If the Commission chooses to make the LLDMS an as-needed service, much of the auction

timing will depend on the type of weather event. A hurricane, for example, can often have some

level of predictability or lead time days or a week or so ahead of landfall. In contrast, a derecho

type event is much less predictable. What may appear to be a normal line of storms can turn severe

without much advanced notice. A set timeframe for preliminary auctions may not be possible in

all cases.


                                                                                                 2
            An as-needed service will require a great deal of administrative flexibility. TEC

recommends that pre-event auctions take place as soon as a threat to the grid with a high likelihood

of occurrence that could potentially result in emergency conditions is identified.

4.         Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so,
           what limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?

           Yes, transmission emergencies that are anticipated to result in load shed should be eligible

for LLDMS deployment.3 As written in statute, the Commission is authorized to deploy the

reliability service “in the event of an anticipated emergency condition.”4 The statute then goes on

to require the Commission to specify the period when the service may be used to assist with

potential reliability issues “during extreme weather events.”5 In TEC’s reading of the statute, this

appears to be a general grant of authority for the Commission to deploy the service for anticipated

emergency conditions, which may extend beyond weather events, but as part of the rule the

Commission must specifically define when the service may be used for reliability purposes during

weather events. For purposes of this service, anticipated emergency conditions should be limited

to those times where ERCOT anticipates exhausting all lower-cost market-based solutions.

                                                 II.       Comments

A.         Remove Extreme Weather Limitations on Program Usage

           The PFP, in TEC’s understanding, limits the use of the LLDMS to extreme weather

conditions, defined as weather conditions likely to result in an Energy Emergency Alert (EEA).6

TEC reiterates its prior position stated in response to Staff’s preliminary questions that the

statutory language does not limit the use of LLDMS to only extreme weather conditions. Rather,


3
    See Responses of Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. at 4 (Apr. 8, 2026).
4
    PURA § 39.170(b).
5
    PURA § 39.170(b)(1).
6
    PFP at 9 – 10; Proposed §25.521(d), (d)(1)(C), (d)(1)(D), and (e)(2).



                                                                                                     3
 the Commission and ERCOT are permitted to use LLDMS to address any emergency condition

but must specifically state when the program would be used to address emergencies that result

from an extreme weather condition.7 TEC recommends removing the phrase “due to an extreme

weather condition” at the following places: proposed §25.521(d), (d)(1)(C), (d)(1)(D), and (e)(2).8

           In order to differentiate the use of LLDMS in response to weather conditions versus during

emergency conditions that are not weather related, such as a transmission emergency, generator or

load trip, inverter-based resource ride through failure, or other non-weather emergency that may

result in EEA, TEC recommends adding subsection (e)(4) to the deployment section that reads as

follows:

                     (e)(4) ERCOT may deploy the LLDMS during an extreme weather

                     condition for the duration of the extreme weather condition until the

                     large load customer can be recalled safely, as determined and

                     communicated by ERCOT.

           TEC believes that the incorporation of this language, combined with the removal of the

“due to extreme weather” clauses, strikes the appropriate balance, allowing the LLDMS to be

deployed during various kinds of emergency situations where load control is a valuable tool and

also sets the guardrail boundaries indicating how the LLDMS will be deployed during an extreme

weather event.

B.         Clarify ERCOT’s Ability to Reject for Prior Failure to Comply

           Proposed subsection (d)(3)(B)(iii) requires ERCOT to reject an LLDMS offer that is

submitted on behalf of a large load that fails to comply with the previous LLDMS obligation



7
    Responses of Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. at 4.
8
    PFP at 9 – 10.



                                                                                                   4
 period.9 It is unclear if this means that any prior failure to comply with LLDMS bars a subsequent

offer, or if only a failure to comply with the most recent LLDMS deployment bars an offer. TEC

recommends that this language be clarified as either a failure to comply with “a previous” or “the

most recent” LLDMS obligation period, depending on the Commission’s intention.

C.         Define QSE Obligations

           ERCOT is required to set up various punishment mechanisms for QSEs that fail to meet

their LLDMS obligations.10 As currently written, the only requirement of the QSE, as it relates to

LLDMS obligations, is to submit offers on behalf of large load customers. 11 If there are other

obligations contemplated by the Commission for the QSEs to follow, which would result in

potential enforcement actions from the Commission, those should be stated clearly within the

proposed rule or in ERCOT protocols.

D.         Treatment of LLDMS Loads in Load Shed

           The PFP does not address the treatment of LLDMS loads that are responding to program

directives and impacts on required load shed by the interconnecting Transmission Service Provider

(TSP) or Distribution Service Provider (DSP). In the event that a large load is participating in

LLDMS and is already offline, this should be accounted for and credited towards the TSP/DSP

load shed obligations. If left unclarified, this could leave service providers in a position where they

are unable to meet load shed obligations and subject to ERCOT penalties.

           As an example, a DSP with 500 MW of total load and a 300 MW large load that participates

in LLDMS leaves only 200 MW of load that the DSP can shed. If the 300 MW large load is left

unaccounted for and not either credited to the DSP’s load shed obligation or at least backed out of


9
    PFP at 10.
10
     PFP at 12; Proposed §25.251(g)(1).
11
     PFP at 10; Proposed §25.251(d)(3).



                                                                                                     5
 the DSP’s total load, the DSP may be unable to meet certain load shed obligations. If the DSP is

instructed to shed 50% of its load, but ERCOT still looks at the total 500 MW of load, this would

require the DSP to shed 250 MW of load with only 200 actual MW available to shed. It is

impossible for the DSP to comply with ERCOT’s instruction in this scenario.

       There are two potential solutions to this quandary. First, ERCOT can account for the large

load’s LLDMS participation prior to load shed by backing the large load’s MWs out of the DSP’s

total. In the example above, rather than the 500 MW of total load, ERCOT would subtract the 300

MW of large load and look only at the 200 MW of total load left. A 50% load shed instruction

would therefore only require 100 MW of load shed.

       Second, ERCOT could credit large loads that participate in LLDMS to the load shed

obligation of its DSP and/or TSP. Applied to the same example, ERCOT would still consider the

500 MW total load, so the 50% load shed instruction would still result in 250 MW of necessary

load shed. But in this scenario ERCOT would credit the DSP with 300 MW of pre-existing load

shed through the large load’s participation in LLDMS, meaning no further load shed would be

required.

       TEC does not have a stated preference regarding the treatment of LLDMS-participating

loads during load shed, but TEC does request that such participation be recognized in some way

and that treatment be made clear in the proposed rule.

                                       III.   Conclusion

       TEC appreciates the opportunity to provide comments in response to the PFP and looks

forward to working with the Commission and other stakeholders on this project.

                                   PROJECT NO. 58482

 LARGE LOAD DEMAND                             §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 MANAGEMENT SERVICE                            §
                                               §                    OF TEXAS

                               Texas Electric Cooperatives’
                                  Executive Summary

     Texas Electric Cooperatives makes the following observations and recommendations:

1.   The LLDMS budget should account for both readiness and performance payments that
     incentivize different actions.

2.   Pre-event auctions should take place as soon as a threat to the grid with a high likelihood
     of occurrence that could potentially result in emergency conditions is identified.

3.   Transmission emergencies that are anticipated to result in load shed should be eligible for
     LLDMS deployment.

4.   Anticipated emergency conditions should be limited to those times where ERCOT
     anticipates exhausting all lower-cost market-based solutions.

5.   Remove the extreme weather limitations on program usage and allow LLDMS to be used
     in various emergency conditions anticipated to result in EEA.

6.   Clarify ERCOT’s ability to reject a bid for LLDMS service based on a prior failure to
     comply.

7.   Define any other QSE obligations contemplated by the Commission regarding LLDMS.

8.   ERCOT should account for LLDMS participation by a large load during load shed
     instructions.
